tutorial_example_entry.lesson_title: Geometric Area Methods for Rectangular Pulse Convolution
tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Compute rectangular-pulse convolutions by translating overlap intervals into geometric areas that produce the correct triangular or trapezoidal piecewise output across time.

sections.lesson_title: Geometric Area Methods for Rectangular Pulse Convolution
sections.section_title: Introduction to Geometric Area Methods for Rectangular Pulse Convolution

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean instructional $\tau$-axis signal plot for one fixed time t. Show $x(\tau)$ as a fixed positive rectangular pulse and $h(t - \tau)$ as a shifted positive rectangular pulse on the same $\tau$ axis. Shade only their common nonzero overlap as a rectangle. Label the overlap width $L(t)$, the pulse heights A and B, and the integrand height AB over the shaded overlap region. Keep the visual focused on the fixed-time overlap area; do not include decorative elements or a full piecewise output plot.

blocks.text: The convolution setup already tells us where the two factors are nonzero at a fixed time t. The geometric area method starts with that overlap interval on the $\tau$-axis and turns it directly into the value of the convolution.
In the fixed-time picture, $x(\tau)$ stays fixed while $h(t - \tau)$ is the shifted pulse. Only the $\tau$-values where both rectangles overlap contribute to the integral.

Use the simplest case first: suppose the two positive rectangular pulses overlap on one interval of length $L(t)$. If $x(\tau)$ has height A and $h(t - \tau)$ has height B on that overlap, then the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is constant there with height AB.
So the integral over the nonzero overlap is just the area of a rectangle. Its width is the overlap length, and its height is the product of the pulse amplitudes.

As t changes, the same area rule is reused. The overlap length can grow, stay constant during full overlap, or shrink, and those three behaviors become the pieces of the triangular or trapezoidal convolution output.

sections.section_title: Converting an Overlap Interval into Rectangular Area

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean instructional $\tau$-axis signal plot for one fixed time t. Show two rectangular pulse factors on the same $\tau$ axis: $x(\tau)$ with height 2 and $h(t - \tau)$ with height 3. Shade only their common nonzero overlap interval $1 \le \tau \le 4$. Label endpoints $\tau = 1 and \tau = 4$, overlap width 4 - $1 = 3$, pulse heights 2 and 3, and the constant product height 6 over the shaded overlap. Keep the visual focused on this single fixed-time rectangle-area computation; do not include growing, shrinking, or piecewise output cases.

example_content.example_prompt: At a fixed time, $x(\tau)$ has height 2, $h(t - \tau)$ has height 3, and the two pulses overlap only on $1 \le \tau \le 4$. Use the geometric area method to find the convolution value $y(t)$ at that time.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the overlap interval is already known. Since the factors are rectangular pulses, the convolution value at this fixed time is the area of one rectangle: overlap width times the product of the pulse heights.
First find the width of the shaded overlap. The overlap runs from $\tau = 1$ to $\tau = 4$, so its width is right endpoint minus left endpoint.
Next find the height of the rectangle in the integrand. On the overlap, $x(\tau)$ has height 2 and $h(t - \tau)$ has height 3, so their product is constant with height 6.
Now multiply the rectangle height by the overlap width. That area is the value of the convolution at this fixed time.
So the convolution value at this fixed time is 18.

sections.lesson_title: Geometric Area Methods for Rectangular Pulse Convolution
sections.section_title: Finding Growing and Shrinking Areas for a Triangular Output

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact instructional sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for two equal-width unit-height rectangular pulses of width 2. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 2 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 2 \le \tau \le t as t increases$. Include first contact at $t = 0$, growing partial overlap for $0 < t < 2 with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, full alignment at $t = 2 with overlap length 2$, shrinking partial overlap for $2 < t < 4 with shaded interval [t - 2$, 2] and length 4 - t, and separation at $t = 4$. Label the breakpoints 0, 2, and 4, the unit heights, and the shaded overlap lengths. Keep the visual focused on the triangular equal-width case; do not include unequal-width plateau behavior or nonunit amplitudes.

example_content.example_prompt: Two unit-height rectangular pulses each have width 2. In the $\tau$-axis picture, $x(\tau)$ is supported on $0 \le \tau \le 2$ and $h(t - \tau)$ is supported on $t - 2 \le \tau \le t$. Use geometric area to find the triangular convolution output over the times when the pulses overlap.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the overlap interval is no longer fixed. The same area rule still applies, but the overlap width now changes with t. Since both pulse heights are 1, the convolution value equals the overlap length.
Start by locating the three breakpoints. The shifted support first touches the fixed support at $t = 0$, fully aligns at $t = 2$, and separates at $t = 4$.
On the growing interval, the overlap runs from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = t$. Its width is t, and the unit height product leaves the area equal to that width.
On the shrinking interval, the overlap runs from $\tau = t - 2$ to $\tau = 2$. Its width is the fixed right endpoint minus the moving left endpoint.
Again the unit height product does not change the area, so the falling branch is the shrinking overlap length.
Outside the contact interval, the overlap length is zero. Putting the growing and shrinking areas together gives the triangular convolution output.

explanation_blocks.latex: y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & t<0,\\ t, & 0\le t\le 2,\\ 4-t, & 2\le t\le 4,\\ 0, & t>4.\end{cases}

sections.section_title: Finding Constant Full-Overlap Area for a Trapezoidal Output

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact instructional sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for two unequal-width unit-height rectangular pulses. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 4 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 2 \le \tau \le t as t increases$. Include first contact at $t = 0$, growing partial overlap for $0 < t < 2 with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, full overlap for $2 < t < 4 with the shorter pulse fully inside the longer pulse and shaded length 2$, shrinking partial overlap for $4 < t < 6 with shaded interval [t - 2$, 4] and length 6 - t, and separation at $t = 6$. Label breakpoints 0, 2, 4, and 6, the unit heights, and the plateau caused by the shorter width. Keep the visual focused on the trapezoidal unequal-width case; do not include nonunit amplitudes or unrelated signal shapes.

example_content.example_prompt: A unit-height rectangular pulse of width 4 is convolved with a unit-height rectangular pulse of width 2. In the $\tau$-axis picture, let $x(\tau)$ be supported on $0 \le \tau \le 4$ and $h(t - \tau)$ be supported on $t - 2 \le \tau \le t$. Use geometric area to find the trapezoidal output over the nonzero time interval.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the pulse widths are unequal. The overlap can grow, then hold constant while the shorter pulse is fully inside the longer pulse, then shrink. Since both heights are 1, the convolution value is still just the overlap length.
Use the supports to mark the case changes. First contact occurs at $t = 0$. The shorter pulse becomes fully overlapped at $t = 2$, stops being fully overlapped at $t = 4$, and separates at $t = 6$.
On the growing interval, the overlap runs from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = t$. Its width is t, so the area grows linearly.
On the full-overlap interval, the entire shorter pulse is inside the longer pulse. The overlap length is not changing; it is the shorter width, 2.
On the shrinking interval, the overlap runs from $\tau = t - 2$ to $\tau = 4$. Its width is the fixed right edge minus the moving left edge.
Because the heights are unit heights, that shrinking length is the falling branch of the output. Outside $0 \le t \le 6$, there is no overlap, so the output is zero.

sections.section_title: Applying Pulse Amplitudes to Geometric Area

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean instructional $\tau$-axis diagram for applying amplitudes to known overlap lengths. Show two rectangular pulse factors with height labels 2 and 3, a shaded overlap region labeled $L(t)$, and the product height 2 x $3 = 6 marked over the overlap$. Include two compact labeled cases below or beside the main diagram: $L(t) = t for 0 \le t \le 2 and L(t) = 4 - t for 2 \le t \le 4$. Emphasize that the overlap intervals and breakpoints stay unchanged while the area is scaled by the amplitude product. Do not introduce a plateau case, new support endpoints, or decorative elements.

example_content.example_prompt: Two rectangular pulses have heights 2 and 3. Their overlap length is t for $0 \le t \le 2$ and 4 - t for $2 \le t \le 4$. Use geometric area to write the convolution output on the nonzero intervals.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the overlap-length pieces are already known. This section does not change the time intervals or recompute the geometry; it only scales each overlap length by the product of the pulse heights.
Start with the two overlap-length pieces from the geometry. These are the widths of the shaded overlap region on the two nonzero intervals.
Now compute the height of the rectangle in the integrand. Wherever the pulses overlap, $x(\tau)$ has height 2 and $h(t - \tau)$ has height 3, so their product has height 6.
Use the area rule from the earlier sections: convolution value equals product height times overlap length. The amplitude product multiplies both pieces and leaves the intervals unchanged.
Substitute each overlap-length expression into that rule to get the scaled output on the nonzero intervals.
The breakpoints stay at $t = 0$, $t = 2$, and $t = 4$. Only the vertical scale changes, because the heights multiply the overlap area by 6.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Convolution from Area Cases

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact left-to-right sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for assembling a full piecewise convolution. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 3 with height 2 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 1 \le \tau \le t with height 1$. Include panels for $t < 0 no overlap$, $0 < t < 1 growing partial overlap with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, $1 < t < 3 full overlap with shaded length 1$, $3 < t < 4 shrinking partial overlap with shaded interval [t - 1$, 3] and length 4 - t, and $t > 4 no overlap$. Label breakpoints $t = 0$, 1, 3, 4, amplitude product 2 x $1 = 2$, and the zero-output regions. Keep the image instructional and aligned to the final piecewise assembly; do not include unrelated signal shapes or answer choices.

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(\tau)$ have height 2 on $0 \le \tau \le 3$, and let $h(t - \tau)$ have height 1 on $0 \le t - \tau \le 1$. Use geometric area cases to assemble the complete piecewise formula for $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that this is an assembly problem. Use the support endpoints to find the time cases, use the overlap length in each case, and multiply every nonzero area by the amplitude product.
First write the two supports in the $\tau$-axis picture. The fixed pulse is on [0, 3], and the shifted pulse has width 1 with support [t - 1, t].
The case changes happen at first contact, start of full overlap, end of full overlap, and final separation. Those breakpoints are $t = 0$, $t = 1$, $t = 3$, and $t = 4$.
Next compute the amplitude product. Wherever the pulses overlap, the integrand height is the product of the two rectangular pulse heights.
On the growing interval, the overlap is [0, t], so the overlap length is t. Multiplying by the amplitude product gives the first nonzero piece.
On the full-overlap interval, the entire width-1 pulse is inside the width-3 pulse. The overlap length is constant at 1, so the area is constant.
On the shrinking interval, the overlap is [t - 1, 3]. Its length is the fixed right endpoint minus the moving left endpoint.
Multiplying that shrinking length by the amplitude product gives the final nonzero piece. Before first contact and after final separation, the overlap length is zero.
Now place all pieces in increasing order of t to get the complete piecewise convolution output.

explanation_blocks.latex: y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & t<0,\\ 2t, & 0\le t\le 1,\\ 2, & 1\le t\le 3,\\ 2(4-t), & 3\le t\le 4,\\ 0, & t>4.\end{cases}

Shade only their common nonzero overlap interval $-2 \le \tau \le 1$. prompt_blocks.text: At a fixed time, the graph shows $x(\tau) = 4$ and $h(t - \tau) = 2$ over their common nonzero interval $2 \le \tau \le 6$. Use geometric area to find $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The overlap width is right endpoint minus left endpoint, and the integrand height is the product of the pulse heights.

prompt_blocks.text: At a fixed time, the graph shows $x(\tau) = 3$ and $h(t - \tau) = 5$ over their common nonzero interval $-2 \le \tau \le 1$. Use geometric area to find $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative left endpoint does not change the rule. The overlap width is 1 - (-2), and the rectangle height is the amplitude product.

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact instructional sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for two equal-width unit-height rectangular pulses of width 3. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 3 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 3 \le \tau \le t as t increases$. Include first contact at $t = 0$, growing partial overlap for $0 < t < 3 with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, full alignment at $t = 3 with overlap length 3$, shrinking partial overlap for $3 < t < 6 with shaded interval [t - 3$, 3] and length 6 - t, and separation at $t = 6$. Label the breakpoints 0, 3, and 6, the unit heights, and the shaded overlap lengths. Keep the visual focused on the triangular equal-width case; do not include unequal-width plateau behavior or nonunit amplitudes.

Create a compact instructional sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for two equal-width unit-height rectangular pulses of width 4 with shifted support. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $1 \le \tau \le 5 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 4 \le \tau \le t as t increases$. Include first contact at $t = 1$, growing partial overlap for $1 < t < 5 with shaded interval [1$, t] and length t - 1, full alignment at $t = 5 with overlap length 4$, shrinking partial overlap for $5 < t < 9 with shaded interval [t - 4$, 5] and length 9 - t, and separation at $t = 9$. Label the breakpoints 1, 5, and 9, the unit heights, and the shaded overlap lengths. prompt_blocks.text: Two unit-height rectangular pulses are supported on $0 \le \tau \le 3$ and $0 \le t - \tau \le 3$. Use growing and shrinking overlap areas to write $y(t)$ for the nonzero time interval.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pulses first touch at $t = 0$, fully align at $t = 3$, and separate at $t = 6$. Since both heights are 1, the area equals the overlap length.

prompt_blocks.text: Two unit-height rectangular pulses are supported on $1 \le \tau \le 5$ and $t - 4 \le \tau \le t$. Use growing and shrinking overlap areas to write $y(t)$ for the nonzero time interval.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The fixed support starts at $\tau = 1$ and ends at $\tau = 5$. The moving support first touches at $t = 1$, fully aligns at $t = 5$, and separates at $t = 9$.

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact $\tau$-axis sequence for two unequal-width unit-height rectangular pulse supports. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 5 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 2 \le \tau \le t$. Include first contact at $t = 0$, growing partial overlap for $0 < t < 2 with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, full overlap for $2 < t < 5 with the shorter moving pulse fully inside the longer fixed pulse and shaded length 2$, shrinking partial overlap for $5 < t < 7 with shaded interval [t - 2$, 5] and length 7 - t, and separation at $t = 7$. Label breakpoints 0, 2, 5, and 7, unit heights, and the constant plateau from the shorter width. Do not include nonunit amplitudes, answer choices, or unrelated signal shapes.

Create a compact $\tau$-axis sequence for two unequal-width unit-height rectangular pulse supports where the moving support is longer than the fixed support. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 3 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 5 \le \tau \le t$. Include first contact at $t = 0$, growing partial overlap for $0 < t < 3 with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, full overlap for $3 < t < 5 with the shorter fixed pulse fully inside the longer moving pulse and shaded length 3$, shrinking partial overlap for $5 < t < 8 with shaded interval [t - 5$, 3] and length 8 - t, and separation at $t = 8$. Label breakpoints 0, 3, 5, and 8, unit heights, and the constant plateau from the shorter width. Do not include nonunit amplitudes, answer choices, or unrelated signal shapes.

prompt_blocks.text: A unit-height rectangular pulse $x(\tau)$ is supported on $0 \le \tau \le 5$, and the shifted unit-height pulse $h(t - \tau)$ is supported on $t - 2 \le \tau \le t$. Use geometric area cases to write $y(t)$ over the nonzero time interval.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=t$ for $0 \le t \le 2$, $y(t)=2$ for $2 \le t \le 5$, and $y(t)=7-t$ for $5 \le t \le 7$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shorter pulse has width 2, so the overlap grows until $t = 2$, stays constant at length 2 until $t = 5$, and then shrinks until $t = 7$.

prompt_blocks.text: A unit-height rectangular pulse $x(\tau)$ is supported on $0 \le \tau \le 3$, and the shifted unit-height pulse $h(t - \tau)$ is supported on $t - 5 \le \tau \le t$. Use geometric area cases to write $y(t)$ over the nonzero time interval.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=t$ for $0 \le t \le 3$, $y(t)=3$ for $3 \le t \le 5$, and $y(t)=8-t$ for $5 \le t \le 8$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Here the fixed pulse is the shorter width, so the plateau height is 3. The overlap grows from $t = 0$ to $t = 3$, is fully overlapped from $t = 3$ to $t = 5$, and shrinks to zero by $t = 8$.

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean instructional $\tau$-axis diagram for applying amplitudes to known triangular overlap lengths. Show two rectangular pulse factors with height labels 4 and 1/2, a shaded overlap region labeled $L(t)$, and the product height 4 x $1/2 = 2 marked over the overlap$. Include two compact labeled cases: $L(t) = t for 0 \le t \le 3 and L(t) = 6 - t for 3 \le t \le 6$. Emphasize that the breakpoints stay 0, 3, and 6 while the overlap lengths are scaled by the amplitude product. Do not introduce a plateau case, new support derivation, answer choices, or decorative elements.

Create a clean instructional $\tau$-axis diagram for applying amplitudes to known trapezoidal overlap lengths. Show two rectangular pulse factors with height labels 3 and 2, a shaded overlap region labeled $L(t)$, and the product height 3 x $2 = 6 marked over the overlap$. Include three compact labeled cases: $L(t) = t for 0 \le t \le 2$, $L(t) = 2 for 2 \le t \le 5$, and $L(t) = 7 - t for 5 \le t \le 7$. Emphasize that the breakpoints stay 0, 2, 5, and 7 while every area piece is scaled by the same amplitude product. Do not introduce new support derivation, answer choices, or decorative elements.

prompt_blocks.text: The overlap length for two rectangular pulses is $L(t) = t$ on $0 \le t \le 3$ and $L(t) = 6 - t$ on $3 \le t \le 6$. If the pulse heights are 4 and 1/2, use geometric area to write $y(t)$ on the nonzero intervals.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude product is 4 times 1/2, which equals 2. Multiply both overlap-length pieces by 2 and keep the same breakpoints.

prompt_blocks.text: The overlap length for two rectangular pulses is $L(t) = t$ on $0 \le t \le 2$, $L(t) = 2$ on $2 \le t \le 5$, and $L(t) = 7 - t$ on $5 \le t \le 7$. If the pulse heights are 3 and 2, use geometric area to write $y(t)$ on the nonzero intervals.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)$=6t for $0 \le t \le 2$, $y(t)=12$ for $2 \le t \le 5$, and $y(t)=6$(7-t) for $5 \le t \le 7$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude product is 3 times 2, which equals 6. Multiply the growing, constant, and shrinking overlap-length pieces by 6 without moving any breakpoints.

image_slots.image_description: Create a compact left-to-right sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for assembling a full piecewise convolution. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $0 \le \tau \le 4 with height 3 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 2 \le \tau \le t with height 2$. Include panels for $t < 0 no overlap$, $0 < t < 2 growing partial overlap with shaded interval [0$, t] and length t, $2 < t < 4 full overlap with shaded length 2$, $4 < t < 6 shrinking partial overlap with shaded interval [t - 2$, 4] and length 6 - t, and $t > 6 no overlap$. Label breakpoints $t = 0$, 2, 4, 6, amplitude product 3 x $2 = 6$, and the zero-output regions. Keep the image instructional and aligned to final piecewise assembly; do not include unrelated signal shapes or answer choices.

Create a compact left-to-right sequence of $\tau$-axis overlap snapshots for assembling a full shifted-support piecewise convolution. Show $x(\tau)$ fixed on $1 \le \tau \le 5 with height 1 and h(t - \tau) supported on t - 2 \le \tau \le t with height 3$. Include panels for $t < 1 no overlap$, $1 < t < 3 growing partial overlap with shaded interval [1$, t] and length t - 1, $3 < t < 5 full overlap with shaded length 2$, $5 < t < 7 shrinking partial overlap with shaded interval [t - 2$, 5] and length 7 - t, and $t > 7 no overlap$. Label breakpoints $t = 1$, 3, 5, 7, amplitude product 1 x $3 = 3$, and the zero-output regions. Emphasize that the first contact is shifted to $t = 1$; do not include unrelated signal shapes or answer choices.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(\tau)$ have height 3 on $0 \le \tau \le 4$, and let $h(t - \tau)$ have height 2 on $0 \le t - \tau \le 2$. Use geometric area cases to write the complete piecewise formula for $y(t)$, including where it is zero.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=0$ for $t<0$, $y(t)$=6t for $0 \le t \le 2$, $y(t)=12$ for $2 \le t \le 4$, $y(t)=6$(6-t) for $4 \le t \le 6$, and $y(t)=0$ for $t>6$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shifted support is [t - 2, t], so the breakpoints are 0, 2, 4, and 6. The amplitude product is 6, which scales the growing length t, the full-overlap length 2, and the shrinking length 6 - t.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: y(t)=\begin{cases}0, & t<0,\\ 6t, & 0\le t\le 2,\\ 12, & 2\le t\le 4,\\ 6(6-t), & 4\le t\le 6,\\ 0, & t>6.\end{cases}

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(\tau)$ have height 1 on $1 \le \tau \le 5$, and let $h(t - \tau)$ have height 3 on $0 \le t - \tau \le 2$. Use geometric area cases to write the complete piecewise formula for $y(t)$, including where it is zero.

questions.correct_answer: $y(t)=0$ for $t<1$, $y(t)=3$(t-1) for $1 \le t \le 3$, $y(t)=6$ for $3 \le t \le 5$, $y(t)=3$(7-t) for $5 \le t \le 7$, and $y(t)=0$ for $t>7$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The fixed support begins at $\tau = 1$, so first contact is at $t = 1$. The overlap lengths are t - 1, then 2, then 7 - t, and the amplitude product 1 times 3 scales each nonzero piece.
